(Surah al-Muzzammil)
It has twenty verses and was revealed in Mecca.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O you who are wrapped up,﴾ ﴿stand [in prayer] during the night﴾

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ — concerning this there are two issues.

The first issue: The scholars agree that the one addressed by al-Muzzammil is the Prophet (ﷺ). Its original form is al-mutazammil, with a tā' (taʾ), meaning one who wraps himself in his garments, i.e., wraps himself up in them. The tā' was assimilated into the zāy, and similarly al-muddaththir is from al-mutadaththir. The scholars differed over why he wrapped himself in his garment, and they gave several explanations:

The first: Ibn ʿAbbas said: When Jibril (peace be upon him) first came to him, he was frightened of him and thought that he had been touched by a jinn. So he returned from the mountain trembling and said, "Wrap me up (zammilūnī)." While he was in that state, Jibril came and called him, saying, "O you who are wrapped up."

The second: al-Kalbi said: The Prophet (peace be upon him) only wrapped himself in his garments in order to prepare himself for prayer. This is the view chosen by al-Farrāʾ.

The third: He (peace be upon him) was sleeping at night, wrapped in a qaṭīfa (a blanket), so he was called by something that reproaches that state. It was said: "O you who sleep wrapped in your garment, arise and occupy yourself with worship."

The fourth: He was wrapped in a cloak belonging to Khadijah, finding comfort in it, so it was said to him: ﴿O you who are wrapped up, stand [in prayer] during the night﴾, as if it were said: leave aside the portion of the self and occupy yourself with worship.

The fifth: ʿIkrimah said: "O you who has been burdened (zummila) with a great matter," i.e., who has borne it. Al-zaml means a load, and izdamalahu means he bore it.

The second issue: ʿIkrimah read (al-muzammil and al-muddaththir) with a light zāy and dāl and a heavy mīm and thāʾ, as an active or passive participle. If it is in the active participle form, the object is omitted, and the meaning is "O you who wraps himself (nafsahu), and you who covers himself (nafsahu)." Omitting the object in such a context is eloquent, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿and she has been given of everything﴾ [al-Naml: 23], meaning she has been given something of everything. If it is in the passive form, then it means that he was wrapped by himself or that someone else wrapped him. It was also read as "O you who wraps himself" (al-mutazammil), according to the original form.

As for His saying, ﴿stand [in prayer] during the night﴾, concerning it there are two issues:

[Page 152]

The first issue: Ibn ʿAbbas said: Standing in prayer during the night was an obligation upon the Messenger of Allah, because of His saying: ﴿stand [in prayer] during the night﴾, and the apparent meaning of a command is obligation. Then it was abrogated (nusikha). They differed over the cause of the abrogation, in several views:

The first: It was obligatory before the five daily prayers were enjoined, and then it was abrogated by them.

The second: When He, the Exalted, said: ﴿stand [in prayer] during the night, except a little, half of it, or reduce it a little, or add to it﴾, a man did not know how much he had prayed or how much of the night remained, so he would stand the whole night for fear that he might not preserve the required amount. This was hard on them, to the point that their feet and shins swelled. Then Allah the Exalted abrogated that by His saying at the end of this surah: ﴿So recite what is easy of it﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20], and that was in the early days of Islam. Then Ibn ʿAbbas said: Between the first imposition of this and its abrogation there was a year. In another narration he said: The imposition of this was in Mecca and its abrogation was in Medina. Then this amount was also abrogated by the five prayers. The difference between this view and the first view is that in this view the obligation of tahajjud was abrogated by His saying: ﴿So recite what is easy of the Qur'an﴾, and then this was abrogated by the imposition of the prayers; whereas in the first view, the obligation of tahajjud was abrogated directly by the imposition of the five prayers.

Some scholars said: Tahajjud was never obligatory at all, and the evidence for this is several points:

The first: His saying: ﴿And from the night, perform tahajjud with it as a supererogatory prayer for you﴾ [al-Isra': 79], which makes clear that tahajjud is a supererogatory (nafilah) prayer for him, not an obligation. Ibn ʿAbbas answered this by saying that the meaning is an additional obligation upon you.

The second: If tahajjud had been obligatory upon the Messenger, it would have been obligatory upon his community, because of His saying: (and follow him) [al-A'raf: 158], and the occurrence of abrogation is contrary to the original principle.

The third: Some who argue for the non-obligation cited His saying: ﴿half of it, or reduce it a little, or add to it﴾, by which the determination was left to the discretion of the one obligated; and what is like this is not obligatory. This is weak, because it is not far from reason to say: "I have obligated upon you standing in prayer at night, but its measure, whether less or more, is left to your judgment." Then those who hold that it is not obligatory answered the argument from His saying: ﴿stand [in prayer] during the night﴾, and said: The apparent meaning of a command indicates recommendation (nadb), because we have seen that the commands of Allah the Exalted sometimes indicate recommendation and sometimes indicate obligation, so it is necessary to take it as indicating the common element between the two forms, to avoid homonymy and metaphor. This is nothing but preferring the side of doing over the side of abstaining. As for the permissibility of abstaining, it is established by the basic principle. So when preference was achieved by the command and permissibility of abstaining was achieved by the basic principle, that is the recommended (mandub). And Allah knows best.

The second issue: Abu al-Sammal read "qum al-layl" (with a fatha on the mīm), while others read it with a ḍamma on the mīm. Abu al-Fath Ibn Jinni said: The purpose of this vowel is to avoid the meeting of two sukūns (consonants at rest), so whichever vowel is used, the purpose is achieved. Qutrub related from them: qum al-layl, and qul al-ḥaqq (with raised mīm and lām), and biʿ al-thawb. Then he said: Whoever kasra'd, it is on the original principle; whoever ḍamma'd, he followed (the vowel of the next letter); and whoever fatha'd, he inclined to the lightness of fatha.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 73, verse 2–3:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Except a little,﴾ ﴿half of it, or diminish from it a little,﴾ ﴿or add to it﴾.

Know that people have said much in the interpretation of this verse, and I have two summarized views on it:

The first: The intended meaning of His saying ﴿except a little﴾ is a third (al-thuluth). The evidence for this is His saying, exalted is He, at the end of this surah: ﴿Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand (in prayer) almost two-thirds of the night, or half of it, or a third of it﴾. This verse shows that the largest of the obligatory measures is two-thirds, and this indicates that sleeping for a third is permissible. If that is the case, then it is necessary that the intended meaning in His saying ﴿Stand (in prayer) the night, except a little﴾ is a third. Accordingly, His saying ﴿Stand (in prayer) the night, except a little﴾ means: stand for two-thirds of the night. Then He said ﴿half of it﴾, and the meaning is: or stand half of it, just as you say: "Sit with al-Hasan or Ibn Sirin," meaning: sit with this one or that one, whichever you wish, deleting the conjunctive waw. So the construction of the verse is: stand two-thirds, or stand half, or diminish from the half, or add to it. On this basis, two-thirds is the maximum of the addition and a third is the maximum of the reduction. Thus the obligatory is a third, and what exceeds it is recommended (mandub). If it is said: On this interpretation, it follows for you that the Prophet ﷺ abandoned an obligation, because He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand (in prayer) almost two-thirds of the night, and half of it, and a third of it﴾. Whoever reads (nisfihi wa thuluthihi) with the genitive (al-khafd), the meaning is that you stand less than two-thirds, less than half, and less than a third. If a third is obligatory, then he, peace be upon him, would be abandoning an obligation. We say: They used to estimate the third by ijtihad, so they may have erred in that ijtihad and fallen short of it by a little, and so that would be less than a third of the night as known by the precise determination of the parts with God. For this reason He, exalted is He, said to them: ﴿He knows that you will not be able to keep count of it﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20].

The second view: That His saying "half of it" is an explanation of His saying "a little." This explanation is permissible for two reasons:

The first: Half of a thing is little in relation to its whole.

The second: If the obligation is half, its bearer does not come out of the responsibility of that duty with certainty except by adding something little to it, so it becomes in reality half and something more, and what remains after that is less than it. Given this, we say: ﴿Stand (in prayer) the night, except a little﴾ means: stand the night except half of it, so the result is: stand half the night. Then He said ﴿or diminish from it a little﴾, meaning: or diminish from this half its half, until a quarter remains. Then He said ﴿or add to it﴾, meaning: or add to this half its half, so that the total becomes three-quarters. In that case the sum of the verse returns to this: He, exalted is He, gave him the choice between standing a full half, or standing a quarter of the night, or standing three-quarters of it. On this reckoning, the obligation that cannot be avoided is standing a quarter, and what exceeds it is among the recommended acts and supererogatory voluntary prayers. On this interpretation the problem you mentioned is entirely resolved, because His saying ﴿Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand (in prayer) almost two-thirds of the night, and half of it, and a third of it﴾ indicates that he, peace and blessings be upon him, did not stand two-thirds of the night, nor half of it, nor a third of it; since the obligation was only a quarter, abandoning the standing for a third does not entail abandoning any of the obligations. Thus the question mentioned is removed. And God knows best.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And recite the Qur'an in measured recitation﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "Recite the Qur'an in measured recitation" means make it clear with a clear articulation (*tabyin*). Thus, upon reaching the mention of God, one feels His greatness and majesty; and upon reaching the promise and the threat, hope and fear arise, and then the heart is illumined by the light of knowing God. Hastening in recitation indicates a lack of standing upon the meanings, because the soul rejoices in mentioning the divine, spiritual matters, and whoever rejoices in something loves to mention it, and whoever loves something does not pass over it quickly. So it becomes clear that the purpose of *tartil* is only the presence of the heart and the perfection of knowledge.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 73, verse 5:

They have mentioned several interpretations of "heavy" (al-thaqil) in the tafsir (exegesis):

The first, which is my preferred view, is that what is meant by its being heavy is the greatness of its station and the magnificence of its significance. Everything that is precious and of great value is called *thiql*, *thaqil* and *thaqil* (heavy). This is the meaning of Ibn 'Abbas's statement in the narration of 'Ata': ﴿a heavy word﴾, meaning a great speech. As for the connection of the verse (wajh al-nazm), when God, exalted is He, commanded him to pray at night, it was as if He said: "I have only commanded you to pray at night because We shall cast upon you a great word, so you must strive to make yourself ready for that great word. This readiness is not attained except through night prayer. For when a person, in a dark night, occupies himself with the worship of God, turns to His remembrance, praise and humble supplication before Him, and there is none of the sensory distractions or bodily obstacles, the soul becomes prepared to be illuminated by the majesty of God, and it becomes ready for complete detachment and the greatest unveiling within the limits of human capacity. Since night prayer has an effect in making the soul ready for this meaning, He therefore said: 'I have only commanded you to pray at night because We shall cast upon you a heavy word, so prepare your soul to receive that meaning.' The completion of this meaning is what the Prophet, upon him be peace, said: 'Indeed, your Lord has breaths of grace (nafahat) in the days of your life; so expose yourselves to them.'"

The second: They said: what is meant by the heavy word is the Qur'an and what it contains of commands and prohibitions, which are burdensome obligations for mukallafin (accountable persons) in general, and for the Messenger of God in particular, because he bears them himself and conveys them to his community. Its essence is that its heaviness returns to the heaviness of acting upon it, for there is no meaning to obligation except the imposition of that whose performance involves hardship and difficulty.

The third: It was narrated from al-Hasan that it is heavy in the scale on the Day of Resurrection. This points to the abundance of its benefits and the abundance of reward in acting upon it.

The fourth: What is meant is that he, upon him be peace, would become heavy (weighed down) when revelation descended upon him. It was narrated that revelation descended upon him while he was on his she-camel, and it became heavy upon her, until she lowered her young, and she could not move.

And from Ibn 'Abbas: when revelation descended upon him, it weighed upon him and his face would darken. And from 'A'isha, may God be pleased with her: "I saw revelation descending upon him on a very cold day, and it would withdraw from him, and his forehead would be dripping with sweat."

The fifth: al-Farra' said: "a heavy word" means it is neither light nor trivial, because it is the speech of our Lord, blessed and exalted.

The sixth: al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is that it is a firm word in its soundness, its clarity and its benefit, just as you say: "This is a weighty speech (kalam razin), and this is a word that has weight, when you admire it and know that it has been placed in its proper position of wisdom and clarity."

The seventh: Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: it is heavy upon the hypocrites, in that it exposes their secrets, and in that it nullifies their religions and their claims.

The eighth: The heavy thing, by its nature, remains in its place and does not move. So "heavy" was used as a metaphor (kinaya) for the permanence of the Qur'an throughout time, as He said: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Reminder, and indeed We are its guardians﴾ [al-Hijr: 9].

The ninth: It is heavy in the sense that a single intellect cannot fully grasp its benefits and meanings. The theologians have plunged into the seas of its rational meanings, the jurists have turned to investigating its rulings, and likewise the experts in language, grammar and rhetoric. Then every later scholar continues to gain benefits from it that earlier scholars did not reach. Thus we know that a single human being cannot independently bear it, and it becomes like a heavy burden that creation is unable to carry.

The tenth: It is heavy because it contains the muhkam (clear, unambiguous verses) and the mutashabih (ambiguous verses), and the abrogating (nasikh) and the abrogated (mansukh). The distinction between these categories is something that only the firmly grounded scholars (al-rasikhun fi al-'ilm), who encompass all the rational and judicial sciences, are capable of. Since this is so, comprehending it is necessarily burdensome for the majority of creation.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 73, verse 6:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the rising of the night﴾. It is said: "nashat-a tansha'u nash'an," so she is "nashi'ah" (rising). Al-insha' (bringing into being) is al-ihdath (causing to occur). So everything that comes into being is called "nashi'" for the masculine and "nashi'ah" for the feminine. Having understood this, we say that regarding al-nashi'ah there are two opinions:

The first: it is an expression for the hours of the night.

The second: it is an expression for the matters that occur during the hours of the night.

As for the first opinion, Abu 'Ubaydah said: "Nashi'at al-layl are its hours and its successive, consecutive parts, for they come into being one after another, so one is a nashi'ah after another nashi'ah." Then those who hold this view differed. Some of them said: the whole night is nashi'ah. Ibn Abi Mulaykah narrated: "I asked Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr about nashi'at al-layl, and they both said: the whole night is nashi'ah."

Zayn al-'Abidin, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Nashi'at al-layl is what is between Maghrib and 'Isha'," and this is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak and al-Kisa'i. They said: "Because nashi'at al-layl is the hour from which the darkness of the night begins."

The second opinion: it is the interpretation of al-nashi'ah as matters that arise in the night. On this view they mentioned several aspects:

The first: they said: "nashi'at al-layl" is the soul that rises during the night, which gets up from its bed to worship, that is, it rises and ascends, from "nasha'at al-sahabah" when the cloud rose.

The second: nashi'at al-layl is an expression for standing in prayer at night after sleep. Ibn al-A'rabi said: "If you sleep a sleep at the beginning of the night and then get up, that is the nash'ah, and from it comes nashi'at al-layl."

I have in this a third aspect: that when a person turns to worship and remembrance at night, in a dark house, in a place where his senses do not become occupied with any sensible thing whatsoever, then the heart turns to spiritual thoughts and divine reflections. As for the day, the senses are occupied with sensible things, so the soul becomes occupied with sensible things and is not free for spiritual states. So what is meant by nashi'at al-layl is those spiritual inspirations and luminous thoughts that are revealed in the darkness of the night because of the emptiness of the senses. He named them nashi'at al-layl because they occur only at night, since the senses that preoccupy the soul are idle at night and busy during the day. It is not mentioned that those things arising from them are sometimes thoughts and reflections, sometimes lights and unveilings, and sometimes psychic emotions of joy in the world of holiness or fear of it, or imaginings of wondrous states. Since those arising matters are many kinds that no single comprehensive term gathers, yet they are arising, newly occurring matters, for this reason He described them only as nashi'at al-layl.

* *

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿is more intense﴾, meaning more in agreement, more suitable, and more in accord. It is a verbal noun; one says: "wati'tu fulanan 'ala kadha muwata'atan wa wat'ah," and from it comes ﴿so that they may agree upon the number of what Allah has forbidden﴾ [al-Tawbah: 37], meaning so that they may conform. If we interpret al-nashi'ah as the hours, the meaning is that they are more in agreement with what is intended of humility and sincerity. If we interpret it as the rising soul, the meaning is the intensity of agreement between heart and tongue. If we interpret it as standing in prayer at night, the meaning is what is intended of humility and sincerity. If we interpret it according to what I mentioned, the meaning is that the attainment of those struggles to the occurrence of unveilings at night is more intense than during the day. And from al-Hasan: more in agreement between the secret and the public, because the sight of creatures is cut off.

The second issue: it was read "ashadda wat'an" with fath and kasr, and in it there are two views:

The first: al-Farra' said: "More firm in footing, because people are restless and move about during the day to earn their living."

The second: heavier and harsher upon the one praying than prayer during the day, from your saying: "ishtaddat 'ala al-qawm wat'at sultanihim" when their dealings with him became burdensome to them. And in the hadith: "O Allah, make Your trampling heavy upon Mudar." So Allah informed His Prophet that the reward for standing in prayer at night is in proportion to the intensity and weight of the trampling. A parallel to this is his saying, upon him be prayer and peace: "The best of acts of worship is the most arduous of them," meaning the most difficult. Abu 'Ubaydah preferred the first reading. He said: because when He commanded him to stand at night, He mentioned this verse, as if He said: "I only commanded you to pray at night because agreement of heart and tongue in it is more complete, and also the nocturnal thoughts lead more fully to spiritual unveilings."

* *

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and more upright in speech﴾. In it there are two issues:

The first issue: ﴿and more upright in speech﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "more beautiful in utterance." Ibn Qutaybah said: because at night voices subside, movements cease, and speech becomes pure, with no barrier between it and being heard and understood.

The second issue: Anas read "wa-aswabu qilan" (and more correct in speech). It was said to him: "O Abu Hamzah, it is only: wa-aqwamu qilan." Anas said: "Asweb and ahya' are one." Ibn Jinni said: this shows that the people used to consider the meanings, and when they found them they did not attend to the wording. A parallel to this is what is reported: Abu Sawwar al-Ghanawi used to read "fa-hasu khilal al-diyar" with an unpointed ha', and it was said to him: "It is only jasu," and he said: "Hasu and jasu are one." I say: that must be understood to mean that he mentioned it as an explanation of the wording of the Qur'an, not that he made it the Qur'an itself. For if we followed what Ibn Jinni said, reliance upon the wording of the Qur'an would be removed, and we would allow that everyone expresses the meaning with a word he sees as matching that meaning, and perhaps he is right in that belief, and perhaps he is wrong, and this leads to attacking the Qur'an. Thus it is established that he understood it in the sense we have mentioned.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 73, verse 7–8:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, for you by day is extensive occupation.﴾ On this there are two issues:

The first issue: Al-Mubarrid said: "Sabhan" means turning about in what is necessary. For this reason the swimmer (sabih) is called "sabih," because of his turning about with his hands and feet. Then, regarding the meaning, there are two views:

The first: Indeed, for you by day there is busy movement and turning about in your important affairs, so you will not be free to serve God except at night. For this reason I have commanded you to pray at night.

The second: Al-Zajjaj said: That is, if you miss something of the night from sleep and rest, then for you in the day there is free time, so devote it to that.

The second issue: It has been read as "sabkhan" with a khaʾ dotted from above (ﺥ). It is a metaphor from "sabakh al-suf" (the carding of wool), which is teasing it out and spreading its parts, for the heart during the day becomes scattered because of preoccupations, and its concerns vary because of the differing causes. Know that He, may He be exalted, first commanded His Messenger to stand in prayer at night, then mentioned the reason why He specified the night for that rather than the day, then explained which of the actions commanded during the night's standing is the most noble.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And mention the name of your Lord and devote yourself to Him with complete devotion.﴾ This verse indicates that God commanded two things:

One of them: remembrance (dhikr).

The second: devotion (tabattul). As for remembrance, know that He said here, "mention the name of your Lord," and in another verse He said, "And mention your Lord within yourself, humbly and in fear" [al-A'raf: 205], because at the beginning of the matter one must mention the Name with the tongue for a period, then the Name passes away while the Named remains. So the first rank is what is meant by His saying here, "mention the name of your Lord."

The second rank is what is meant by His saying in the other surah, "mention your Lord within yourself." You are occupied with the remembrance of the Lord only when you are in the station of contemplating His lordship, and His lordship is an expression of the various kinds of His nurturing you and His kindness to you. So as long as you are in this station, your heart is occupied with contemplating His bounties and blessings, and you are not wholly absorbed in Him. He is the Manifest, for He is the origin of the manifestation of every manifest thing, and He is the Hidden, for He is above the intellects of all creatures. Glory be to Him who is veiled from the intellects by reason of the intensity of His manifestness, and is concealed from them by the perfection of His light.

The first issue: Know that all the exegetes explained "tabattul" as sincerity. Know that when He, exalted is He, first commanded him to remember (the name of his Lord) and then to devote himself wholly to Him (*tabattul*, complete devotion and withdrawal from all else), He mentioned the reason for this, saying, exalted is He: ﴿Lord of the east and the west; there is no god but Him, so take Him as your guardian.﴾ On this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Know that wholehearted devotion (*tabattul*) to Him is only attained after love (*mahabbah*) has been established, and love is fitting only for God, exalted is He. This is because the cause of love is either perfection or the bestowing of perfection. As for perfection, it is loved for its own sake, since it is known that it is impossible for everything to be loved only for the sake of something else, for that would lead to an infinite regress (*tasalsul*). Therefore one must end at that which is loved for its own sake, and perfection is loved for its own sake. Whoever believes that a certain person who lived a thousand years before this was described as having knowledge greater than the knowledge of all other people, his nature inclines toward him and he loves him, whether he wills it or not. And whoever believes that Rustam was described as having a bravery exceeding the bravery of all other people, loves him, whether he wills it or not. Thus we know that perfection is loved for its own sake, and the perfection of perfection belongs to God, exalted is He. So God, exalted is He, is loved for His own sake. Whoever does not have His love established in his heart, that is due to his lack of knowledge of His perfection. As for the bestowing of perfection, it is that the generous one is loved, and the absolutely generous is God, exalted is He. So the absolutely beloved is God, exalted is He, and absolute devotion can only be directed toward God, exalted is He, because absolute perfection belongs to Him and absolute bestowal of perfection comes from Him. Therefore absolute devotion must be directed only to Him.

Know also that the devotion directed to Him because He is the source of bestowing perfection takes precedence over the devotion directed to Him because He is perfect in His essence. This is because a person at the beginning of the journey is seeking a share (*hissah*, a portion of benefit), so his devotion to God, exalted is He, is due to His being the source of perfecting and bestowing. Then at the end of the journey he rises above seeking a share, as we have explained, that he becomes one who seeks the Giver rather than the gifts (*ma'ruf*, the favour), so his devotion in this state is due to His being perfect. Thus His saying ﴿Lord of the east and the west﴾ points to the first state, which is the first of the degrees of those who are devoted, and His saying ﴿there is no god but Him﴾ points to the second state, which is the final degree of those who are devoted and the furthest step of the truthful ones (*al-siddiqin*, those of the highest sincerity). Glory be to He for whom there is a hidden secret beneath every word. Beyond these two states there is another station, which is the station of complete entrusting (*tafwid*), namely that one removes choice from between (oneself and God) and entrusts the matter entirely to Him. If the Real intends for him to become devoted, he is content with devotion, not because it is his own (*min haythu innahu huwa*), but because it is the will of the Real. And if He intends for him not to be devoted, he is content with non-devotion, not because it is non-devotion, but because it is the will of the Real. Here is the last of the degrees. His saying ﴿so take Him as your guardian﴾ points to this state. This is what the pen has written in the interpretation of this verse, and in the corners there are hidden things, and among the secrets of this verse there are remainders. ﴿And if whatever trees are on the earth were pens and the sea, replenished by seven seas after it, were ink, the words of God would not be exhausted.﴾ [Luqman: 27]

**The second issue:** The word *Rabb* (Lord) has two readings (*qira'at*, the recognized modes of recitation).

The first is the nominative (*raf'*), and it has two aspects:

One: it is in the sense of praise, and the implied sense is "He is the Lord of the east," so it is the predicate of an omitted subject, as in His saying ﴿Worse than that is the Fire﴾ [al-Hajj: 72], and His saying ﴿a little enjoyment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 179], meaning: their turning about is a little enjoyment.

The second: you take it as the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is the clause ﴿there is no god but Him﴾, and the returning pronoun to it is the detached pronoun (*al-damir al-munfasil*, the independent pronoun, "Him/He").

The second reading is the genitive (*khafd*), and in it there are two aspects:

The first: it is in apposition (*badal*) to "your Lord."

The second: Ibn 'Abbas said: it is an oath, by the omission of the particle of oath, as when you say: "By God, I will certainly do it," and its answer is ﴿there is no god but Him﴾, just as you say: "By God, there is no one in the house except Zayd." Ibn 'Abbas also read: "Lord of the easts and the wests."

As for His saying ﴿so take Him as your guardian﴾, the meaning is that since it is established that there is no god but Him, it is necessary for you to take Him as your guardian and to entrust all your affairs to Him. Here is a great station. For since knowing that there is no god but Him requires entrusting all matters to Him, this shows that whoever does not entrust all matters to Him does not truly know the reality of "there is no god but Him." Its explanation: everything other than Him is contingent and originated, and everything contingent and originated does not come into existence unless it ends at the Necessary Existent in Himself. Since the Necessary Existent in Himself is one, all contingent things are dependent upon Him and terminate in Him. This is what is meant by His saying ﴿so take Him as your guardian﴾. Some of them said: "(a guardian)" means: a surety (*kafil*) for what He has promised you of victory and triumph.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 73, verses 10–11:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And bear patiently what they say, and part from them with gracious parting.﴾ The meaning: since you have taken Me as your Trustee (wakil), then bear patiently what they say and entrust their affair to Me. For since I am your Trustee, I take charge of setting right your affair better than you take charge of setting right the affairs of your own self. Know that the essential concerns of servants are confined to two matters: the manner of their dealings with God, and the manner of their dealings with creation. The first is more important than the second. So when He, exalted is He, mentioned at the beginning of this surah what relates to the first category, He followed it with what relates to the second category. He, glorified is He, gathered in these two words everything that is needed in this domain. That is because a person is either mixing with people or keeping aloof from them. If he mixes with them, he must be patient in the face of their harm and their alienating him. For if he hopes from them for good and comfort and does not find it, he falls into griefs and sorrows. Thus it is established that whoever wishes to mix with creation must have much patience. As for if he abandons mixing, that is the gracious parting. Thus it is established that every person must have one of these two matters. The gracious parting is that he keeps aloof from them in his heart and desire, and opposes them in deeds, along with forbearance, overlooking, and abandoning retaliation. Its parallels are: ﴿So turn away from them and admonish them﴾ [al-Nisa': 63], ﴿And turn away from the ignorant﴾ [al-A'raf: 199], ﴿So turn away from one who turns his back on Our remembrance﴾ [al-Najm: 29]. The exegetes said: this verse was revealed before the verse of fighting, then it was abrogated (nusikha) by the command to fight. Others said: rather, that is the taking of what is more conducive to acceptance by God's permission, so abrogation does not apply to its like, and this is more sound.

﴿And leave Me with the deniers, the people of luxury, and give them respite a little.﴾

Know that when a person is concerned with an important matter, and another is able to fully and perfectly suffice for that matter, he says to him: "Leave me and that," meaning: there is no need, given my concern with that, for anything else. It is like His saying: ﴿So leave Me with whoever denies this discourse﴾ [al-Qalam: 44]. As for His saying: ﴿the people of luxury (ulī al-ni'mah)﴾: with a fatha (on the nun), it means luxurious living; with a kasra, it means bestowing favour; with a damma, it means delight. It is said: "an'ama bika" and "na'imaka 'aynan," meaning: it gladdened your eye. They are the chieftains of Quraysh, who were people of luxury and affluence. ﴿And give them respite a little﴾: concerning this there are two views:

The first: by "a little" is meant the life of this world.

The second: by "a little" is meant that brief period remaining until the Day of Badr, for God destroyed them on that day.

Know that I do not say that what is meant by these verses is only what I have mentioned; rather I say: they indicate the occurrence of the four corporeal levels and the occurrence of the four spiritual levels, and there is no barrier to interpreting them as both, although the wording is literal with respect to the corporeal levels and figurative, well-known and established, with respect to the spiritual levels.

The answer: Yes, because the statement is only coherent if we analogize one of the two cases to the other. Then it would be necessary to analogize all other analogies to this analogy, and that would be establishing qiyas by qiyas, which is not permissible. We reply: We do not establish all other analogies by analogy to this case, for otherwise the undesirable consequence you mentioned would follow. This affirmation must be taken to have been preceded by the premise that whenever sharing in an apparent operative cause occurs, sharing in the ruling must be affirmed, and that the mere possibility of a distinction based on things whose relevance to the ruling is not known does not undermine that equality. So there is no meaning to our saying "qiyas is a proof" except this.

The answer: Because the people of Makkah looked down upon Muhammad (ﷺ) and held him in contempt because he was born among them, just as Pharaoh looked down upon Musa because he was raised and born among them. Then Allah, exalted is He, returned to warning them about the Resurrection once more, saying: ﴿How then will you guard yourselves, if you disbelieve, against a Day that will make children grey-haired? The sky will be split asunder by it. His promise is always fulfilled.﴾ And in this there are several issues:

The first issue: al-Wahidi said: In the verse there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), meaning: How will you guard yourselves against a Day that makes children grey-haired, if you disbelieve?

The second issue: The author of al-Kashshaf mentioned several possibilities regarding His saying "yawman" (a Day):

The first: It is an object (maf'ul bihi), meaning: How will you guard your souls on the Day of Resurrection and its terror, if you remain in disbelief?

The second: It is an adverbial of time (zarf), meaning: How will you have taqwa (God-consciousness) on the Day of Resurrection, if you disbelieve in this world?

The third: It is governed by "kafartum" (you disbelieve), interpreted as "jahadtum" (you deny), meaning: How will you guard yourselves against Allah and fear Him, if you deny the Day of Resurrection and the recompense? For taqwa of Allah has no meaning except fear of His punishment.

The third issue: He, exalted is He, mentioned two aspects of the terror of that Day:

The first: His saying ﴿a Day that makes children grey-haired﴾. In this there are two possibilities:

The first: It is a figurative expression (mathal) for severity, used of a grievous day, "a day when the foreheads of children turn grey." The principle behind it is that when sorrows and griefs accumulate upon a person, greying comes upon him quickly, because the abundance of worries causes the spirit to retreat into the interior of the heart; that retreat extinguishes the innate heat (al-hararah al-gharizziyyah); the extinguishing and weakening of that innate heat leaves the nutritive parts not fully ripened; this causes phlegm to dominate the humours; and this causes the hair to whiten. So when they saw that greying is a necessary consequence of abundant worries, they used greying as a kinayah (metonymy) for severity and affliction. It is not meant that the terror of that Day literally makes children grey-haired, because inflicting pain and fear upon children is not permissible on the Day of Resurrection.

The second: It is permissible that what is meant is a description of that Day as long, and that children reach, in it, the age of old age and greying. Some of the literati asked me about the line of al-Ma'arri:

"And an injustice that fills both temples with grey."

And he said: How is the comparison in the Qur'an preferred over the verse of al-Ma'arri? I said: For several reasons:

The first: That the temples being filled with grey hair is not astonishing; but the children becoming grey-haired is astonishing. It is as if the severity of that Day transports them from the age of childhood to the age of old age, without passing in between the two states through the age of youth. This is the great exaggeration in describing the Day as severe.

Second: The filling of the temples with grey means the whitening of the hair, and hair may whiten due to an illness while the strength of youth remains. So this contains no exaggeration. As for the verse, it indicates the transformation of children into elderly people in weakness, thinness, and the absence of freshness of face, and that is the extreme of the severity of that Day.

Third: The filling of the temples with grey contains no exaggeration, because the sides of the head are a place for abundant phlegmatic moisture; for this reason, greying first occurs at the temples, and after that in the rest of the sides of the head. So the greying of the temples is not an exaggeration; the exaggeration is the greying taking over all parts of the head, indeed all parts of the body, as is mentioned in the verse. And Allah knows best.

The second kind of the terrors of the Day of Resurrection is His saying: ﴿The sky will be split asunder by it.﴾ This is also a description of the Day as severe, and that the sky, despite its magnitude and strength, will be split apart in it; so what do you think of other creatures? Its parallel is His saying: ﴿When the sky is split apart﴾ (82:1). And in this there are two questions:

The first question: Why did He not say "munfatirah" (feminine)? The answer has several aspects:

The first of them: Abu Ubaydah related from Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala': He said ﴿munfatir﴾ and did not say "munfatirah," because its figurative usage (majaz) is that of a roof; you say: "This is the sky of the house."

The second: al-Farra' said: "sama'" (sky) is used both as feminine and masculine, and here it is in the masculine usage. He recited a line of poetry:

"Were the sky to raise a people up to Him, / we would join the stars along with the clouds."

The third: The feminine gender of "sama'" is not real (haqiqi), and whatever is like that may be masculine. The poet said:

"And the eye, with khayri antimony, is kohl-lined."

And al-A'sha said:

"No rain cloud poured its rain, nor did any land bring forth its vegetation."

The fourth: That "sama'" is an entity possessing splitting (dhat infitar), so it is like the locust that spreads, the green tree, and the trunks of palm trees uprooted; and like their saying: "imra'ah mur'id" (a woman who nurses), meaning one who has nursing (dhat rada'), with the masculine form used for the feminine, in the sense of the attribute of possessing the quality.

The second question: What is the meaning of ﴿munfatir bihi﴾? The answer has several aspects:

The first of them: al-Farra' said: The meaning is "munfatir fihi" (it will be split in it).

The second: The "ba'" in "bihi" is like it in your saying: "I split the wood with the axe (qadum), so it split by it" (fatartu al-'ud bi-l-qadum fa-infatara bihi), meaning that it splits because of the severity and terror of that Day, just as a thing splits by that which splits it.

The third: It is permissible that what is meant is: The sky is burdened by it with a burden that leads to its splitting, due to the greatness of that event falling upon it and its fear of it, like His saying: ﴿It weighs heavy upon the heavens and the earth﴾ (7:187).

As for His saying: ﴿His promise is always fulfilled﴾, know that the pronoun in His saying "wa'duhu" (His promise) may refer to the object (al-maf'ul) or may refer to the agent (al-fa'il). As for the first, the meaning is: the promise of that Day is fulfilled; that is, the promise attributed to that Day is necessarily going to occur, because the wisdom and knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, require its occurrence.

As for the second: the meaning is that the promise of Allah is certain to happen without doubt, because He, exalted is He, is free from lying. And although Allah, exalted is He, has not been mentioned here, it is still appropriate for the pronoun to refer to Him, since He is known.

Know that He, exalted is He, began at the start of the surah by explaining the states of the happy people (al-su'ada'), and it is known that their states are of two kinds:

One of them: what relates to religion and obedience to the Lord, so He mentioned that first.

The second: what relates to dealings with creation, and He explained that by His saying: ﴿So be patient over what they say, and part from them graciously﴾ (73:10).

As for the wretched, He began by threatening them in a general way, which is His saying: ﴿Leave Me with those who deny﴾ (73:11). Then He mentioned after that the kinds of punishment of the Hereafter. Then He mentioned the punishment of this world, which is the severe seizing in this world. Then He described after that the severity of the Day of Resurrection. At this point the explanation was complete in its entirety, so for this reason He concluded that discourse with His saying:

The second question: What is the meaning of ﴿munfatir bihi﴾? The answer has several aspects:

The first of them: al-Farra' said: The meaning is "munfatir fihi" (it will be split in it).

The second: The "ba'" in "bihi" is like it in your saying: "I split the wood with the axe (qadum), so it split by it" (fatartu al-'ud bi-l-qadum fa-infatara bihi), meaning that it splits because of the severity and terror of that Day, just as a thing splits by that which splits it.

The third: It is permissible that what is meant is: The sky is burdened by it with a burden that leads to its splitting, due to the greatness of that event falling upon it and its fear of it, like His saying: ﴿It weighs heavy upon the heavens and the earth﴾ (7:187).

As for His saying: ﴿His promise is always fulfilled﴾, know that the pronoun in His saying "wa'duhu" (His promise) may refer to the object (al-maf'ul) or may refer to the agent (al-fa'il). As for the first, the meaning is: the promise of that Day is fulfilled; that is, the promise attributed to that Day is necessarily going to occur, because the wisdom and knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, require its occurrence.

As for the second: the meaning is that the promise of Allah is certain to happen without doubt, because He, exalted is He, is free from lying. And although Allah, exalted is He, has not been mentioned here, it is still appropriate for the pronoun to refer to Him, since He is known.

Know that He, exalted is He, began at the start of the surah by explaining the states of the happy people (al-su'ada'), and it is known that their states are of two kinds:

One of them: what relates to religion and obedience to the Lord, so He mentioned that first.

The second: what relates to dealings with creation, and He explained that by His saying: ﴿So be patient over what they say, and part from them graciously﴾ (73:10).

As for the wretched, He began by threatening them in a general way, which is His saying: ﴿Leave Me with those who deny﴾ (73:11). Then He mentioned after that the kinds of punishment of the Hereafter. Then He mentioned the punishment of this world, which is the severe seizing in this world. Then He described after that the severity of the Day of Resurrection. At this point the explanation was complete in its entirety, so for this reason He concluded that discourse with His saying:

Indeed, this is a reminder (﴿إنَّ هَذِهِ تَذْكِرَةٌ﴾). So whoever wills takes a path to his Lord (﴿فَمَن شاءَ اتَّخَذَ إلى رَبِّهِ سَبِيلًا﴾). That is: these verses are reminders comprising all kinds of guidance and direction (﴿فَمَن شاءَ اتَّخَذَ إلى رَبِّهِ سَبِيلًا﴾). And taking a path (ittikhadh al-sabil) is an expression for occupying oneself with obedience and guarding oneself against disobedience.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 73, verse 20:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand [in prayer] almost two-thirds of the night, or half of it, or a third of it, and [so do] a group of those with you﴾. In this there are two issues:

The first issue: What is meant by His saying ﴿almost two-thirds of the night﴾ is less than them. The word adnā (nearer, almost), which means closest, is used metaphorically for "less," because when the distance between two things becomes near, the space between them becomes small, and when it becomes far, the space increases.

The second issue: ﴿wa-nisfahu wa-thuluthahu﴾ has been read in the accusative (naṣb), and the meaning is: you stand less than two-thirds, and you stand half. It has also been read in the genitive (jarr), ﴿wa-nisfihi wa-thuluthihi﴾, meaning: you stand less than two-thirds, and [less than] the half and the third. However, we have explained in the commentary on His saying ﴿Stand [in prayer] through the night, except a little﴾ that it does not follow from this that he, upon him be prayer and peace, was neglecting an obligation. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and a group of those with you﴾, meaning your companions, stand in the night for this stated amount.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah measures the night and the day﴾, meaning that the one who knows the measures of the parts of the night and the day is none other than Allah, Exalted is He.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He knows that you will not be able to keep count of it﴾. In this there are two issues:

The first issue: The pronoun in ﴿you will not be able to keep count of it﴾ refers to an implied verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: He knows that it is not possible for you to count the exact measure of each of the parts of the night and the day, and it is also not possible for you to achieve those measures by way of caution and precaution except with complete hardship. Muqatil said: a man would pray the entire night, out of fear that he would not fulfill what he was commanded of standing [in prayer] that was obligatory upon him.

The second issue: Some have used this as an argument for the imposition of what cannot be borne, on the basis that He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿you will not be able to keep count of it﴾, meaning you will not be able to bear it, and He had indeed imposed it upon them. It may be answered that what is meant is its difficulty, not that they are unable to do it, like the saying of one who says: "I cannot bear to look at so-and-so," when he finds looking at him burdensome.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So He turned to you [in forgiveness]﴾ is an expression for the granting of permission to abandon the stipulated standing [in prayer], like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So He turned to you and pardoned you. So now, have relations with them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187]. The meaning is that He lifted the burden from you in abandoning this act, just as He lifts the burden from the one who repents.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So recite what is easy of the Qur'an﴾. In this there are two opinions:

The first: What is meant by this recitation is the prayer, because recitation is one of the parts of the prayer, so the name of the part is applied to the whole, meaning: pray what is easy for you. Then here there are two views:

The first: al-Hasan said: it means in the Maghrib and 'Isha' prayers. Others said: rather, the obligation of that night prayer (tahajjud) was abrogated and it was made sufficient with what is easy of it, and then that too was abrogated by the five daily prayers.

The second opinion: What is meant by His saying ﴿So recite what is easy of the Qur'an﴾ is the recitation of the Qur'an itself, and its purpose is the study of the Qur'an so that one may be secure from forgetting it. It was said: he should recite one hundred verses. It was said: whoever recites one hundred verses is recorded among the devoutly obedient (qānitīn). It was also said: fifty verses. Some said: rather, a short surah is sufficient, because the removal of the night prayer was only to remove hardship, and there is hardship in abundant recitation, so it is not possible to take it into account. Here there is another discussion, which is what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: the standing in prayer during the night fell away from the companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and became voluntary, and it remained an obligation upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

* Then He, Exalted is He, mentioned the wisdom in this abrogation, so He said, Exalted is He: ﴿He knows that there will be among you those who are ill, and others who travel through the land seeking of Allah's bounty, and others who fight in the way of Allah. So recite what is easy of it, and establish prayer and give zakat﴾.

Know that the sense of this verse is as if it were said: Why did Allah abrogate that? And He said: Because He knew such and such. The meaning is: because of the impossibility of standing [in prayer] for the ill and for those who travel through the land for trade and those who strive in the way of Allah. As for the ill, they are unable to devote themselves to tahajjud because of their illness; as for the travelers and the strivers, they are occupied during the day with arduous labours, so if they did not sleep at night, the causes of hardship would continue upon them. This reason did not exist in the case of the Prophet ﷺ, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, for you by day is extensive occupation﴾. Therefore, the obligation of tahajjud was not abrogated in his case. Among the subtleties of this verse is that He, Exalted is He, equated the strivers with those who travel in search of lawful livelihood. And it is related from Ibn Mas'ud: "Whoever brings something to a city of the cities of the Muslims, patiently and seeking reward, and sells it at the price of its day, he is among the martyrs in the sight of Allah." Then He repeated His saying ﴿So recite what is easy of it﴾ a second time, and that is for emphasis. Then He said: ﴿and establish prayer﴾, meaning the obligatory prayer, ﴿and give zakat﴾, meaning the obligatory zakat. It was said: the zakat of fitr, because there was no zakat in Mecca, and it became obligatory only after that. Whoever interprets it as the obligatory zakat makes the end of the surah Medinan.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And lend to Allah a goodly loan﴾. In this there are three aspects:

The first: that it means all voluntary charities.

The second: that it means paying zakat in the best manner, which is giving it from the best and most beneficial of wealth to the poor, observing the intention, seeking the face of Allah, and directing it to the deserving recipient.

The third: that it means every act of good that is done, of what relates to the self and wealth.

* *
Then He, Exalted is He, mentioned the wisdom in giving wealth, so He said: ﴿And whatever good you put forward for yourselves, you will find it with Allah, better and greater in reward. And seek forgiveness of Allah; indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. In this there are two issues:

The first issue: Ibn 'Abbas said: you will find it with Allah better and greater in reward than that which you delay until your bequest at death. al-Zajjaj said: "And whatever good you put forward for yourselves, you will find it with Allah, it is better for you than the goods of this world." The view stated by Ibn 'Abbas is the correct one.

The second issue: The meaning of the verse: "And whatever good you put forward for yourselves, you will find it with Allah, better and greater in reward," except that He said "it is better" for emphasis and exaggeration. Abu al-Sammal read: "huwa khayrun wa-a'zamu ajran" with nominative case, as subject and predicate. Then He said: ﴿And seek forgiveness of Allah﴾ for your sins and the shortcomings proceeding from you, especially in the standing of the night, ﴿indeed, Allah is Forgiving﴾ of the sins of the believers, ﴿Merciful﴾ toward them. Regarding "al-Ghafur" there are two opinions:

One of them: that He is Forgiving of all sins; this is the view of Muqatil.

The second: that He is Forgiving to one who persists in sin. Muqatil argued for his view with two aspects:

The first: that His saying ﴿Forgiving, Merciful﴾ encompasses both the penitent and the persistent, on the evidence that it is valid to make an exception of each of them separately from it, and the ruling of an exception is to exclude what, without it, would have been included.

The second: that forgiveness of the penitent is obligatory according to the opponent, and no praise is achieved by performing an obligation, whereas the purpose of the verse is to establish praise; therefore it must be understood as covering all, to realize the praise. And Allah, glorified and exalted is He, knows best. Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and blessings and peace upon the best of the messengers, Muhammad the Prophet, and his family and all his companions.
